questions.stem: In probability, an event is best described as:
options: a set of outcomes, which is a subset of the sample space
the list of every outcome the experiment could have
a single trial of the experiment and its recorded result
the number of times an outcome occurs in many trials
questions.explanation: An event is a collection of outcomes, so it is a subset of the sample space. The list of every possible outcome is the sample space itself.

questions.stem: A spinner numbered 1 to 5 is spun once. Which outcomes make up the event "an odd number"?
questions.explanation: The sample space is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and the odd outcomes in it are 1, 3 and 5. The number 7 is not a possible outcome, so it cannot belong to any event.

questions.stem: Two coins are tossed. Which outcomes make up the event "exactly one head"?
questions.explanation: The sample space is HH, HT, TH, TT. Exactly one head occurs in HT and TH, which are different outcomes. Including HH would give "at least one head".

questions.stem: Two fair dice are rolled. How many outcomes are in the event "the sum is 10"?
questions.explanation: The outcomes are (4, 6), (5, 5) and (6, 4). Counting (4, 6) and (6, 4) as one outcome gives 2, but they are different results for the two dice.

questions.stem: A family has three children, and each outcome lists the sexes in birth order, such as GBG. How many outcomes are in the event "at least two girls"?
questions.explanation: The sample space has 2³ = 8 outcomes. At least two girls means GGB, GBG, BGG or GGG, which is 4 outcomes. Leaving out GGG gives 3, which is "exactly two girls".

questions.stem: Two students are chosen from Ali, Bree, Chen, Dev and Ella. How many outcomes are in the sample space, and how many in the event "Ali is chosen"?
questions.explanation: The order of choosing does not matter, so the sample space has ⁵C₂ = 10 pairs. Ali is in a pair with each of the other 4 students. The value 20 counts each pair twice, in both orders.

questions.stem: A card is drawn from a standard pack of 52. How many outcomes are in the event "a heart that is a jack, queen or king"?
questions.explanation: The event needs both conditions, so the outcomes are the jack, queen and king of hearts: 3 cards. The value 12 counts all the picture cards, and 22 counts the cards that are hearts or picture cards, which is the union.

questions.stem: For an event A in a sample space ξ, the complement A′ is:
options: every outcome in A that is also in ξ
the outcomes in A that occur most often
every outcome in ξ that is not in A
questions.explanation: The complement A′ (also written Ā) contains every outcome in the sample space that is not in A. Together, A and A′ make up the whole sample space.

questions.stem: The event A ∩ B contains the outcomes that are:
options: in A but not in B
in A or B or both
questions.explanation: The intersection A ∩ B is the set of outcomes common to both events, read "A and B". The outcomes in A or B or both form the union A ∪ B.

questions.stem: The event A ∪ B contains the outcomes that are:
options: in A or B or both
in both A and B only
in exactly one of A and B
questions.explanation: The union A ∪ B, read "A or B", includes outcomes in either event, including those in both. Outcomes in exactly one of the events exclude the intersection.

questions.stem: Which notation means the same as A′?
questions.explanation: Both A′ and Ā denote the complement of A. The sets A ∩ ξ and A ∪ ∅ are both just A itself.

questions.stem: A fair die is rolled. A is "an even number" and B is "a number greater than 3". Which outcomes are in A ∩ B?
questions.explanation: A contains 2, 4, 6 and B contains 4, 5, 6, so the outcomes in both are 4 and 6. The list 2, 4, 5, 6 is the union.

questions.stem: A fair die is rolled. A is "an even number" and B is "a number greater than 3". Which outcomes are in A ∪ B?
questions.explanation: The union lists each outcome in A or B once: 2, 4, 5 and 6. Outcomes in both events are not repeated, and 1 is in neither event.

questions.stem: A fair die is rolled. A is "an even number" and B is "a number greater than 3". Which outcomes are in A′ ∩ B?
questions.explanation: A′ contains the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, and B contains 4, 5, 6, so A′ ∩ B is 5 only. The list 1, 3, 5 is A′ on its own.

questions.stem: A fair die is rolled. A is "an even number" and B is "a number greater than 3". Which outcomes are in (A ∪ B)′?
questions.explanation: A ∪ B contains 2, 4, 5 and 6, so its complement is 1 and 3. Including 5 forgets that 5 is in B and so in the union.

questions.stem: R is the event "it rains on Saturday" and S is "it rains on Sunday". What does R′ ∩ S′ describe?
options: It does not rain on either day
It rains on at least one of the days
It does not rain on both days
It rains on exactly one of the days
questions.explanation: R′ ∩ S′ means "not R and not S", so it is dry on both days. "Not raining on both days" is (R ∩ S)′, which still allows rain on one day.

questions.stem: R is the event "it rains on Saturday" and S is "it rains on Sunday". Which event is "it rains on Saturday but not on Sunday"?
questions.explanation: "But" joins two conditions that must both hold, so it is an intersection: rain on Saturday (R) and no rain on Sunday (S′). R ∪ S′ would also include days when it is dry both days.

questions.stem: R is the event "it rains on Saturday" and S is "it rains on Sunday". Which event is "it rains on at least one of the two days"?
questions.explanation: At least one day means Saturday or Sunday or both, which is the union R ∪ S. R ∩ S needs rain on both days.

questions.stem: R is the event "it rains on Saturday" and S is "it rains on Sunday". Which event is "it rains on exactly one of the two days"?
questions.explanation: Exactly one day means rain Saturday and not Sunday, or rain Sunday and not Saturday. (R ∩ S)′ also includes the case of no rain at all, and R ∪ S also includes rain on both days.

questions.stem: For any events A and B, which set is always equal to (A ∪ B)′?
questions.explanation: An outcome is outside A ∪ B exactly when it is outside A and outside B, so (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′. The set A′ ∪ B′ equals (A ∩ B)′, which is larger.

questions.stem: A is the event x > 2 and B is the event x ≤ 5, where x is a real number. What is A ∩ B?
questions.explanation: The intersection is where both conditions hold: x greater than 2 and at most 5. The union of the two events is every real number, and x ≤ 2 or x > 5 is the complement of the intersection.

questions.stem: Events A and B are mutually exclusive when:
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events have no outcomes in common, so their intersection is the empty set. A ∪ B = ξ means that together they cover the sample space, which is a different property.

questions.stem: A fair die is rolled once. Which pair of events is mutually exclusive?
questions.explanation: The outcome 1 is not even, so "a 1" and "an even number" cannot happen together. Each other pair shares an outcome: 2, then 1 and 3, then 6.

questions.stem: A card is drawn from a standard pack. Are the events "a king" and "a heart" mutually exclusive?
options: Yes, because kings and hearts are different features
Yes, because only one card is drawn from the pack
No, because there are more hearts than kings in the pack
No, because the king of hearts belongs to both events
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events share no outcomes, but the king of hearts is in both events. The numbers of cards in each event do not decide whether they overlap.

questions.stem: A fair die is rolled. Which pair of events is mutually exclusive but NOT complementary?
questions.explanation: "Less than 3" (1, 2) and "greater than 4" (5, 6) share no outcomes, but 3 and 4 belong to neither, so together they do not make up the sample space. Each other pair is complementary: mutually exclusive and covering every outcome.

questions.stem: For any event A in a sample space ξ, which statement is true?
options: A and A′ overlap, and A ∩ A′ = A
A and A′ are mutually exclusive and A ∪ A′ = ξ
A and A′ are mutually exclusive and A ∩ A′ = ξ
A and A′ overlap, and A ∪ A′ = ξ
questions.explanation: No outcome is both in A and not in A, so A ∩ A′ = ∅, and every outcome is in one or the other, so A ∪ A′ = ξ. This is why P(A′) = 1 − P(A).

questions.stem: Of 40 students, 22 swim, 15 cycle and 6 do both. How many students do neither?
questions.explanation: By inclusion and exclusion, 22 + 15 − 6 = 31 students do at least one, so 40 − 31 = 9 do neither. The value 3 comes from forgetting to subtract the 6 who were counted twice.

questions.stem: Of 40 students, 22 swim (S), 15 cycle and 6 do both. How many students are in the Venn diagram region for "swim only"?
questions.explanation: The 22 swimmers include the 6 who also cycle, so 22 − 6 = 16 swim only. The value 22 is the whole circle for S, not the part outside the overlap.

questions.stem: In a Venn diagram of events A and B, the region inside B but outside A is:
questions.explanation: Inside B means B, and outside A means A′; both must hold, so the region is A′ ∩ B. A ∩ B′ is the region inside A but outside B.

questions.stem: In a sample space, n(A ∪ B) = 50, n(A) = 32 and n(B) = 27. What is n(A ∩ B)?
questions.explanation: From n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B), 50 = 32 + 27 − n(A ∩ B), so n(A ∩ B) = 59 − 50 = 9. The values 18 and 23 are n(A only) and n(B only) after a slip.

questions.stem: Of 40 students, 22 swim (S), 15 cycle (C) and 6 do both. A student is chosen at random. What is P(S′ ∩ C)?
questions.explanation: S′ ∩ C is "cycles but does not swim", which is 15 − 6 = 9 students, so the probability is 9/40. The value 25/40 is P(S′), all students who do not swim.

questions.stem: A committee of 3 is chosen at random from 4 women and 3 men. What is the probability that all three are women?
questions.explanation: The sample space has ⁷C₃ = 35 equally likely committees, and the event "all women" has ⁴C₃ = 4 of them, so P = 4/35. The value 4/7 is the chance that a single person chosen is a woman.

questions.stem: A committee of 3 is chosen at random from 4 women and 3 men. How many outcomes are in the event "at least one man"?
questions.explanation: The complement of "at least one man" is "all women", which has ⁴C₃ = 4 outcomes, so 35 − 4 = 31 committees have at least one man. The value 18 counts committees with exactly one man.

questions.stem: Two tiles are drawn together from six tiles numbered 1 to 6. What is the probability that both numbers are even?
questions.explanation: There are ⁶C₂ = 15 equally likely pairs, and ³C₂ = 3 of them use two of the even tiles 2, 4 and 6, so P = 3/15 = 1/5. The value 1/4 assumes the two draws are independent, as with replacement.

questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed 5 times. How many outcomes in the sample space have exactly 2 heads, and what is the probability of this event?
questions.explanation: Choosing which 2 of the 5 tosses are heads gives ⁵C₂ = 10 outcomes out of 2⁵ = 32, so P = 10/32 = 5/16. The binomial coefficient ⁵C₂ is the entry 10 in row 5 of Pascal's triangle.

questions.stem: A sample space has 6 outcomes. Counting the empty set and the whole sample space, how many different events (subsets) are there?
questions.explanation: The number of events with k outcomes is ⁶Cₖ, and the sum of row 6 of Pascal's triangle, 1 + 6 + 15 + 20 + 15 + 6 + 1, is 2⁶ = 64. The value 720 is 6!, which counts orderings, not subsets.
